newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE - "PowerBeam" could clean up cars.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - "PowerBeam" could clean up cars.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
Even the most devoted environmentalist might end up loving the car if a new device called the "PowerBeam" can help cut emissions and the use of fuel.

Christopher Ellis, chief executive of the British firm XKF Developments, believes fly-wheel technology can be used to store electricity in "hybrid" cars and trucks. Hybrid vehicles have two power plants -- a diesel or petrol engine for highway driving, and emission-free electric motors for city use.

The PowerBeam fly-wheel stores power in the same way that elastic bands provide power for model aircraft. By twisting the propellor, the elastic band becomes tighter and tighter, effectively storing energy. When released, the elastic band unravels, turns the propellor and plane flies off.
Ellis says his PowerBeam concept for storing kinetic energy will bring dramatic fuel savings as part of a hybrid propulsion system.

The PowerBeam system uses rotors mounted parallel to drive shafts for the length of the vehicle. The system winds up unused energy as vehicles free-wheel down gradients. This is unleashed for use in electric motors when required. The system also captures energy released by braking and stores it as electricity for later use.
Currently, hybrid systems use chemical batteries to store power.
QUEST FOR ACCEPTABLE BATTERY
But the battle for the better battery is still far from won.
"The inherent and probably insurmountable limitations of chemical batteries are holding back the introduction of electric vehicles," Ellis said.

"There is also mounting evidence that the full environmental cost of battery manufacture and replacement will overwhelm the benefit of zero local emissions," said Ellis, after addressing a session of the International Symposium on Automotive Technology and Automation held here last week.
Fuel cell power boosted by fly-wheel electricity storage is the ultimate way to go, according to Ellis.
FLYWHEEL DANGERS OVERCOME BY POWERBEAM

PowerBeam also promises to answer safety questions surrounding traditional fly-wheels. What happens after the inevitable catastrophic accident? A flywheel breaking loose or exploding could cause mayhem in a town centre pile-up.
According to Ellis, the length of the PowerBeam and the fact that it would be part of the vehicle's chassis will keep it contained.

"We'll be putting PowerBeam into a truck by the spring of next year, we don't expect a car until three years or so. Testing, testing, testing; there will be hundreds of them put into prototypes and nasty things done to them to ensure safety," Ellis said.

PowerBeam will help the drive to more than double the efficiency of engines. Ellis pointed to Toyota Motor's recent announcement of a hybrid gasoline-electric powered small car which experts say could deliver almost 80 miles (125 km) per gallon.
SKF, URENCO PARTNERS WITH XKF
Sweden's AB SKF, the world's largest bearings maker, and Urenco are partners in PowerBeam. Urenco, one third owned by British Nuclear Fuels, makes and develops centrifuges for uranium separation.
Ellis said XKF is in initial discussions with several U.S. and European manufacturers.
"We'll see PowerBeam in commercial vehicles first followed by luxury cars," he said.
"It must have a characteristic that is strikingly better. We are talkng about a factor of two over conventional methods. That will get everybody's attention."
FINITE FOSSIL FUEL RESERVES SPUR NEW TECHNOLOGY
Ellis said the search for ever cleaner and more economical vehicles is bound to intensify, with even the U.S. government showing concern about the depletion of oil reserves.
"The U.S. wants to get the point when it is shockproof to a major uplift in oil costs," he said.
"It may be 40 years before we run out of oil, but it will probably 25 to 30 before it is blindingly obvious to people and then the prices will really start jacking up."

"So that's the most benign scenario. It also assumes that the Chinese don't go over the top for motorcars. You ain't seen nothing yet in terms of global demand for motor vehicles and the pressure on fossil fuels," Ellis said.

Earlier at the conference Daimler-Benz said the world's car fleet might hit 1.6 billion in 2030 compared with 700 million in 1990 and 800 million in 1995, spurred by new buyers in Asia and Latin America.
